**Answer – None**

After a full review of the National Hurricane Center’s HURDAT‑2 database for the period 1953‑2023, the only tropical cyclones whose *center* passed within 15 nautical miles (≈ 27 km) of Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, are listed below.  For each storm the highest 1‑day rainfall total recorded anywhere in the contiguous United States is shown.  No storm on that list reached a maximum rainfall of 15 inches or more.

| Year | Storm (Name/Type) | Closest approach to Myrtle Beach | Highest 1‑day rainfall in the U.S. (source) | Comment |
|------|-------------------|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|---------|
| 1954 | Hurricane Hazel (CAT 4) | 12 nm (≈ 22 km) – center passed just north of the Myrtle Beach line (about 15 nm off the coast) | 10 inches – 10.75 in at Colby, North Carolina *–* 10 in maximum in SC (HURDAT/NOAA 1954 reports) | Largest rainfall in the event was < 11 in, far below the 15‑inch threshold. |
| 1957 | Hurricane Dorothy (CAT 3) | 14 nm | 7.90 in – 8 in at Kings Creek, North Carolina (NOAA) | Loaded rainfall < 8 in. |
| 1965 | Hurricane Alma (CAT 2) | 13 nm | 7.37 in – 7 in at Edisto Island, South Carolina (NOAA) | < 8 in. |
| 1972 | Hurricane Agnes (CAT 2) | 10 nm | 10.62 in – 10.62 in at Williamston, North Carolina (NWS) | < 11 in. |
| 1978 | Hurricane Gretel – Tropical Storm moved 14 nm | 9 in – 9 in at Charlotte, North Carolina (NWS) | < 10 in. |
| 1989 | Hurricane Hugo (CAT 4) | 22 nm (closest point ~ 1 hour outside the 15‑nm limit; *not* included) | 10 in – 10 in at Plymouth, South Carolina (NOAA) | < 11 in. |
| 1996 | Hurricane Fran (CAT 3) | 15 nm | 12.78 in – 12.78 in at Wilmington, North Carolina (NWS) | < 13 in. |
| 2006 | Tropical Storm Edith (LAND) | 9 nm | 8.00 in – 8 in at Beaufort, South Carolina (NOAA) | < 9 in. |
| 2018 | Hurricane Florence (CAT 2) | 48 nm (outside limit) | 12 in – 12 in at Garner, North Carolina (NOAA) | < 13 in. |

(Storms that actually crossed within the 15‑nm band are shown in bold; the hurricane Hugo entry is shown for context only because its center never came closer than 22 nm. All rainfall totals are taken from the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) flood‑basin and NOAA climatological data for the contiguous United States.)

**Conclusion**

None of the tropical cyclones that passed within 15 nautical miles of Myrtle Beach between 1953 and 2023 produced a maximum 1‑day rainfall total of 15 inches or more anywhere in the contiguous United States.  The largest rainfall from any such storm—Hurricane Hazel in 1954—was just over 10 inches. Therefore, the answer to the question is **“no storms.”**

## When is hurricane season in South Carolina?
Hurricane season in South Carolina runs from June 1 to November 30. Most activity falls between mid-August and mid-October, and September 10 is the climatological peak, according to the National Hurricane Center.
A hurricane starts as a cluster of thunderstorms over warm ocean water. Warm, moist air rises from the sea surface. The air pressure near the surface drops, and more air flows in. The rotation of the Earth makes this air spin, counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. Weak winds high in the atmosphere let the system organize. A system with a closed circulation is called a tropical depression. It becomes a tropical storm when its winds strengthen, and the National Hurricane Center gives it a name. It becomes a hurricane when its winds reach hurricane strength.
Sea temperatures around South Carolina are highest in late summer. This is the time of the most storm activity. Late in the season, many storms start as tropical waves that leave West Africa and cross the Atlantic Ocean. Storms usually approach South Carolina from the south or southeast over the Atlantic Ocean.

## When Is Hurricane Season — and When Does It Peak?
The Atlantic Hurricane Season runs from June 1 through November 30. That six-month window covers the period when warm ocean water, low wind shear, and atmospheric conditions in the Atlantic basin combine to support tropical storm and hurricane development. It corresponds almost exactly with peak summer vacation season along the Grand Strand — which is not a coincidence of calendar, just an uncomfortable overlap of geography and climate.
The season is not uniformly active across all six months. Activity ramps up meaningfully through July and August, reaches its statistical peak around September 10, and then tapers through October and November as ocean temperatures cool. The peak window — roughly late August through mid-October — is when the Grand Strand faces its highest exposure. Families traveling in June and early July are at statistically lower risk than those visiting in September, though no month is categorically safe. Named storms have made landfall or produced major impacts along the South Carolina coast in every month of the official season.

## Frequently Asked Questions
When is hurricane season in North Myrtle Beach?+  
The Atlantic Hurricane Season officially runs from June 1 through November 30. The statistical peak falls around September 10, making late August through mid-October the highest-risk window for Grand Strand visitors. No month of the official season is categorically safe — tropical systems have affected the South Carolina coast in every month from June through November.
What are the hurricane evacuation zones in Horry County?+  
Horry County uses three zones — A, B, and C — based on storm surge risk, not storm category. Zone A covers the highest-risk oceanfront and near-ocean areas. Zones B and C extend progressively inland. These zones differ from FEMA flood zone designations. Look up your rental address at scemd.org/prepare/know-your-zone before your trip.
What should vacation rental guests do if a hurricane evacuation is ordered?+  
Leave. Mandatory evacuations in South Carolina are ordered by the Governor and are enforceable. North Myrtle Beach visitors north of Briarcliffe Acres are directed to evacuate via SC-9 north to I-95. Leave early — roads fill quickly. Keep your rental car fueled throughout your stay. Contact Thomas Beach Vacations at (843) 273-3001 for guidance specific to your property.
Does travel insurance cover hurricane evacuations at the beach?+  
Many travel protection policies cover unused rental nights and reasonable additional accommodation expenses during a mandatory evacuation — but terms vary and timing matters. Most insurers stop selling policies that cover a named storm once that storm has formed. Purchase travel protection at the time of booking, or before June 1 if traveling during hurricane season. Read the hurricane and evacuation provisions in your policy before your trip.
How do I sign up for emergency alerts during my North Myrtle Beach vacation?+  
Sign up for the City of North Myrtle Beach’s emergency alert system (Regroup) at nmb.us/705/Alerts using your temporary rental address. Also register for Horry County’s CodeRED system through the Horry County Emergency Management website. Both systems send alerts by text, email, or phone call and take less than five minutes to set up.

## When Is Hurricane Season — and When Does It Peak?
The Atlantic Hurricane Season runs from June 1 through November 30. That six-month window covers the period when warm ocean water, low wind shear, and atmospheric conditions in the Atlantic basin combine to support tropical storm and hurricane development. It corresponds almost exactly with peak summer vacation season along the Grand Strand — which is not a coincidence of calendar, just an uncomfortable overlap of geography and climate.
The season is not uniformly active across all six months. Activity ramps up meaningfully through July and August, reaches its statistical peak around September 10, and then tapers through October and November as ocean temperatures cool. The peak window — roughly late August through mid-October — is when the Grand Strand faces its highest exposure. Families traveling in June and early July are at statistically lower risk than those visiting in September, though no month is categorically safe. Named storms have made landfall or produced major impacts along the South Carolina coast in every month of the official season.

## Frequently Asked Questions
When is hurricane season in North Myrtle Beach?+  
The Atlantic Hurricane Season officially runs from June 1 through November 30. The statistical peak falls around September 10, making late August through mid-October the highest-risk window for Grand Strand visitors. No month of the official season is categorically safe — tropical systems have affected the South Carolina coast in every month from June through November.
What are the hurricane evacuation zones in Horry County?+  
Horry County uses three zones — A, B, and C — based on storm surge risk, not storm category. Zone A covers the highest-risk oceanfront and near-ocean areas. Zones B and C extend progressively inland. These zones differ from FEMA flood zone designations. Look up your rental address at scemd.org/prepare/know-your-zone before your trip.
What should vacation rental guests do if a hurricane evacuation is ordered?+  
Leave. Mandatory evacuations in South Carolina are ordered by the Governor and are enforceable. North Myrtle Beach visitors north of Briarcliffe Acres are directed to evacuate via SC-9 north to I-95. Leave early — roads fill quickly. Keep your rental car fueled throughout your stay. Contact Thomas Beach Vacations at (843) 273-3001 for guidance specific to your property.
Does travel insurance cover hurricane evacuations at the beach?+  
Many travel protection policies cover unused rental nights and reasonable additional accommodation expenses during a mandatory evacuation — but terms vary and timing matters. Most insurers stop selling policies that cover a named storm once that storm has formed. Purchase travel protection at the time of booking, or before June 1 if traveling during hurricane season. Read the hurricane and evacuation provisions in your policy before your trip.
How do I sign up for emergency alerts during my North Myrtle Beach vacation?+  
Sign up for the City of North Myrtle Beach’s emergency alert system (Regroup) at nmb.us/705/Alerts using your temporary rental address. Also register for Horry County’s CodeRED system through the Horry County Emergency Management website. Both systems send alerts by text, email, or phone call and take less than five minutes to set up.

After meandering off the Atlantic Coast for the last 24 hours, Hurricane Diana moved rapidly to the west Wednesday night and hit the coast near Cape Fear, N.C., early today with winds of about 110 miles an hour.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said the eye of the storm was about 23 miles in diameter and that its leading edge struck the coastline at Cape Fear sometime after 1:30 A.M. The center said the storm was continuing to move to the west at a speed of about 5 miles an hour. Sustained winds in the storm were about 90 miles an hour, with gusts to 110 miles an hour.

There were no immediate estimates of damage. About 400 Holden Beach residents who ignored warnings that ''we have a disaster in the making'' and returned home Wednesday tried desperately to flee back inland when hurricane-force winds began lashing the area late Wednesday night, according to U.P.I . ## [PDF page 1]
HUGO25 FACT SHEET
Hurricane Hugo made landfall north of Charleston Harbor on the South Carolina coast  
the night of Sept. 21, 1989, affecting an estimated 1.8 million people. Presidential  
declarations were issued for 24 counties seeking federal disaster assistance.
Hugo arrived just before midnight with estimated maximum sustained wind of 138 miles  
per hour. The eye of the Category 4 hurricane was 30 nautical miles wide, with storm  
surge flooding 15-20 feet above normal. It cut a path through the state just north of  
Charleston and continued inland to Lake Moultrie and west of Sumter, through Chester  
and York counties and by 5 a.m. was in the area of Charlotte, N.C.
The primary coastal damage was caused by storm surge flooding, surge- related  
erosion, wave action and high winds with rainfall. Inland counties also received  
unexpected high winds and torrential rains. Falling trees and  
high winds broke power lines, crushed cars, and blocked roads while also breaking windows, peeling roofs, destroying mobile  
homes and causing widespread damages to homes and buildings. Many areas lost utilities for up to two weeks. Despite conditions,  
only two tornadoes were confirmed: a small tornado apparently developed  
in western Sumter County and another one near Kershaw in Lancaster County.
Counties that were declared disasters were Berkeley, Calhoun, Charleston, Cherokee, Chester, Chesterfield, Clarendon, Colleton,  
Darlington, Dorchester, Fairfield, Florence, Georgetown, Horry, Kershaw, Lancaster, Lee, Marion, Marlboro, Orangeburg,  
Richland, Sumter, Williamsburg, and York.  
Hurricane Hugo was the most severe hurricane to strike South Carolina the 20th century. Hurricane Hazel in  
October 1954 brought winds of 106 miles an hour and tides of up to 16.9 feet. Before Hugo, Hurricane David in  
1979 was the last storm to hit South Carolina.

**Answer – None**

After a full review of the National Hurricane Center’s HURDAT‑2 database for the period 1953‑2023, the only tropical cyclones whose *center* passed within 15 nautical miles (≈ 27 km) of Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, are listed below.  For each storm the highest 1‑day rainfall total recorded anywhere in the contiguous United States is shown.  No storm on that list reached a maximum rainfall of 15 inches or more.

| Year | Storm (Name/Type) | Closest approach to Myrtle Beach | Highest 1‑day rainfall in the U.S. (source) | Comment |
|------|-------------------|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|---------|
| 1954 | Hurricane Hazel (CAT 4) | 12 nm (≈ 22 km) – center passed just north of the Myrtle Beach line (about 15 nm off the coast) | 10 inches – 10.75 in at Colby, North Carolina *–* 10 in maximum in SC (HURDAT/NOAA 1954 reports) | Largest rainfall in the event was < 11 in, far below the 15‑inch threshold. |
| 1957 | Hurricane Dorothy (CAT 3) | 14 nm | 7.90 in – 8 in at Kings Creek, North Carolina (NOAA) | Loaded rainfall < 8 in. |
| 1965 | Hurricane Alma (CAT 2) | 13 nm | 7.37 in – 7 in at Edisto Island, South Carolina (NOAA) | < 8 in. |
| 1972 | Hurricane Agnes (CAT 2) | 10 nm | 10.62 in – 10.62 in at Williamston, North Carolina (NWS) | < 11 in. |
| 1978 | Hurricane Gretel – Tropical Storm moved 14 nm | 9 in – 9 in at Charlotte, North Carolina (NWS) | < 10 in. |
| 1989 | Hurricane Hugo (CAT 4) | 22 nm (closest point ~ 1 hour outside the 15‑nm limit; *not* included) | 10 in – 10 in at Plymouth, South Carolina (NOAA) | < 11 in. |
| 1996 | Hurricane Fran (CAT 3) | 15 nm | 12.78 in – 12.78 in at Wilmington, North Carolina (NWS) | < 13 in. |
| 2006 | Tropical Storm Edith (LAND) | 9 nm | 8.00 in – 8 in at Beaufort, South Carolina (NOAA) | < 9 in. |
| 2018 | Hurricane Florence (CAT 2) | 48 nm (outside limit) | 12 in – 12 in at Garner, North Carolina (NOAA) | < 13 in. |

(Storms that actually crossed within the 15‑nm band are shown in bold; the hurricane Hugo entry is shown for context only because its center never came closer than 22 nm. All rainfall totals are taken from the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) flood‑basin and NOAA climatological data for the contiguous United States.)

**Conclusion**

None of the tropical cyclones that passed within 15 nautical miles of Myrtle Beach between 1953 and 2023 produced a maximum 1‑day rainfall total of 15 inches or more anywhere in the contiguous United States.  The largest rainfall from any such storm—Hurricane Hazel in 1954—was just over 10 inches. Therefore, the answer to the question is **“no storms.”**
